claim: RSPOs 2 and 3 potentiate WNT/β-catenin signaling in cells lacking leucine-rich repeat-containing G-protein coupled receptors (LGRs) 4, 5 and 6.
source: We previously demonstrated that RSPOs 2 and 3 potentiate WNT/β-catenin signaling in cells lacking leucine-rich repeat-containing G-protein coupled receptors (LGRs) 4, 5 and 6 (Lebensohn and Rohatgi, 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work (Lebensohn and Rohatgi, 2018).

claim: Heparan sulfate proteoglycans (HSPGs) act as alternative co-receptors for RSPO3.
source: We now show that heparan sulfate proteoglycans (HSPGs) act as alternative co-receptors for RSPO3 using a combination of ligand mutagenesis and ligand engineering.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from ligand mutagenesis and ligand engineering experiments presented in the manuscript.

claim: Mutations in RSPO3 residues predicted to contact HSPGs impair its signaling capacity.
source: Mutations in RSPO3 residues predicted to contact HSPGs impair its signaling capacity.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing reduced signaling potency of RSPO3 TSP/BR (K/R→E) mutant in Figure 1D and E.

claim: The HSPG-binding domains of RSPO3 can be entirely replaced with an antibody that recognizes heparan sulfate (HS) chains without diminishing WNT-potentiating activity in cultured cells and intestinal organoids.
source: Conversely, the HSPG-binding domains of RSPO3 can be entirely replaced with an antibody that recognizes heparan sulfate (HS) chains attached to multiple HSPGs without diminishing WNT-potentiating activity in cultured cells and intestinal organoids.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing RSPO3 ΔTSP/BR HS20 maintains signaling activity in Figures 2 and 5.

claim: A genome-wide screen for mediators of RSPO3 signaling in cells lacking LGRs 4, 5 and 6 failed to reveal other receptors.
source: A genome-wide screen for mediators of RSPO3 signaling in cells lacking LGRs 4, 5 and 6 failed to reveal other receptors.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from the haploid genetic screen presented in Figure 6 and Supplementary files 4 and 5.

claim: HSPGs are RSPO co-receptors that potentiate WNT signaling in the presence and absence of LGRs.
source: We conclude that HSPGs are RSPO co-receptors that potentiate WNT signaling in the presence and absence of LGRs.
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple experimental data throughout the manuscript, including mutagenesis, ligand engineering, and functional assays.

claim: Mutations that disrupt the RSPO signaling circuit cause structural birth defects, including limb truncations, lung hypoplasia, craniofacial malformations and cardiovascular defects in humans and mice carrying mutations in RSPO2 and RSPO3.
source: Mutations that disrupt the RSPO signaling circuit cause structural birth defects, exemplified by limb truncations, lung hypoplasia, craniofacial malformations and cardiovascular defects seen in humans and mice carrying mutations in RSPO2 and RSPO3 (Aoki et al., 2008; Aoki et al., 2007; Bell et al., 2008; Nam et al., 2007; Szenker-Ravi et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to multiple prior studies.

claim: RSPOs function as niche-derived signals required for the renewal of epithelial stem cells in multiple tissues, including the intestine, skin and bone.
source: In adults, RSPOs function as niche-derived signals required for the renewal of epithelial stem cells in multiple tissues, including the intestine, skin and bone (de Lau et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: RSPOs amplify responses to WNT ligands by simultaneously binding to LGRs 4, 5 or 6 and one of two transmembrane E3 ubiquitin ligases, ZNRF3 or RNF43.
source: The prevailing paradigm of RSPO signaling holds that they amplify responses to WNT ligands by simultaneously binding to two types of receptors at the cell surface: one of three leucine-rich repeat-containing G-protein coupled receptors (LGRs), LGRs 4, 5 or 6 (hereafter referred to jointly as LGRs), and one of two transmembrane E3 ubiquitin ligases, ZNRF3 or RNF43 (Carmon et al., 2011; Chen et al., 2013; de Lau et al., 2011; Glinka et al., 2011; Gong et al., 2012; Peng et al., 2013a; Peng et al., 2013b; Ruffner et al., 2012; Wang et al., 2013; Zebisch et al., 2013; Zebisch and Jones, 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to multiple prior studies describing the prevailing paradigm.

claim: ZNRF3/RNF43 reduce cell-surface levels of WNT receptors, Frizzled (FZD) and LDL Receptor Related Protein (LRP) 5/6 proteins, by direct ubiquitination.
source: ZNRF3/RNF43 reduce cell-surface levels of WNT receptors, Frizzled (FZD) and LDL Receptor Related Protein (LRP) 5/6 proteins, by direct ubiquitination (Hao et al., 2012; Koo et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: RSPOs amplify WNT signaling by inducing the endocytosis of ZNRF3/RNF43, which leads to an increase in the number of WNT receptors at the plasma membrane.
source: RSPOs amplify WNT signaling by inducing the endocytosis of ZNRF3/RNF43, which leads to an increase in the number of WNT receptors at the plasma membrane and consequently an increase in sensitivity to WNT ligands.
evidence: This claim is supported by established knowledge in the field and citations.

claim: RSPO2 and RSPO3 can potentiate WNT signaling in the absence of LGRs 4, 5 and 6.
source: We and others recently made the unexpected discovery that this paradigm is incomplete: RSPO2 and RSPO3 can potentiate WNT signaling in the absence of LGRs 4, 5 and 6, previously considered obligate high-affinity receptors for RSPOs.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from the authors' previous work and other studies.

claim: RSPO2 and RSPO3 can still potentiate WNT signaling in LGR4/5/6KO human haploid cells.
source: Our previous article in eLife demonstrated that RSPO2 and RSPO3 can still potentiate WNT signaling in LGR4/5/6KO human haploid cells (Lebensohn and Rohatgi, 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: RSPO2 and RSPO3 can amplify WNT-mediated signaling in Lgr4/5/6 triple-knockout immortalized fibroblasts.
source: Similarly, RSPO2 and RSPO3 can amplify WNT-mediated signaling in Lgr4/5/6 triple-knockout immortalized fibroblasts (Szenker-Ravi et al., 2018)
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: RSPO2 can potentiate WNT signaling in 293T cells lacking LGR4.
source: and RSPO2 can potentiate WNT signaling in 293T cells lacking LGR4 (Park et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: LGR-independent mode of signaling is the dominant mode of signaling during development of the limbs, lungs and cardiovascular system.
source: This 'LGR-independent' mode of signaling is particularly relevant to RSPO-related birth defects because it appears to be the dominant mode of signaling during development of the limbs, lungs and cardiovascular system (Szenker-Ravi et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Mice carrying loss-of-function mutations in LGRs 4, 5 and 6 do not show limb truncations, lung hypoplasia or craniofacial abnormalities observed in humans and mouse embryos lacking Rspo2.
source: Mice carrying loss-of-function mutations in LGRs 4, 5 and 6 (Lgr4/5/6-/-) do not show either the limb truncations, lung hypoplasia or craniofacial abnormalities observed in humans and mouse embryos lacking Rspo2 (Aoki et al., 2008; Bell et al., 2008; Szenker-Ravi et al., 2018)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: Mice carrying loss-of-function mutations in LGRs 4, 5 and 6 do not show vascular and associated placental defects observed in mouse embryos lacking Rspo3.
source: or the vascular and associated placental defects observed in mouse embryos lacking Rspo3 (Aoki et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: RSPOs contain tandem furin-like domains, FU1 and FU2, that interact with ZNRF3/RNF43 and LGRs, respectively.
source: RSPOs contain tandem furin-like domains, FU1 and FU2, that interact with ZNRF3/RNF43 and LGRs, respectively.
evidence: This claim is supported by established knowledge in the field.

claim: RSPOs contain a thrombospondin type 1 (TSP) domain and a basic region (BR) that interact with heparin and heparan sulfate proteoglycans (HSPGs).
source: They also contain a thrombospondin type 1 (TSP) domain and a basic region (BR) (we refer to them together as the TSP/BR domain) that interact with heparin and heparan sulfate proteoglycans (HSPGs) (Ayadi, 2008; Chang et al., 2016; Nam et al., 2006; Ohkawara et al., 2011; Ren et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: The TSP/BR domain has been considered dispensable to potentiate WNT/β-catenin signaling.
source: The TSP/BR domain has been considered dispensable to potentiate WNT/β-catenin signaling (Glinka et al., 2011; Kazanskaya et al., 2004; Kim et al., 2008)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: The TSP/BR domain is essential for RSPO signaling in the absence of LGRs.
source: but we previously demonstrated that it is essential in the absence of LGRs (Lebensohn and Rohatgi, 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Disruption of EXTL3 reduces LGR-independent RSPO3 signaling by ~80%.
source: We previously reported that disruption of EXTL3, the gene encoding a glycosyltransferase required for the biosynthesis of all HS chains, reduces LGR-independent RSPO3 signaling by ~80% (Lebensohn and Rohatgi, 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Depleting either all SDCs (1-4) or PIGL did not reduce LGR-independent signaling by RSPO3.
source: However, depleting either all SDCs (1-4) or PIGL, an enzyme required for the biogenesis of all GPCs, did not reduce LGR-independent signaling by RSPO3.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from prior work.

claim: Deleting the complete TSP/BR domain of RSPO3 eliminated its ability to potentiate WNT signaling in LGR4/5/6KO cells.
source: We previously showed that deleting the complete TSP/BR domain of RSPO3 eliminated its ability to potentiate WNT signaling in LGR4/5/6KO cells (Lebensohn and Rohatgi, 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: The RSPO3 TSP/BR domain model shows an elongated three-stranded fold stabilized by disulfide bonds at both ends.
source: Analogous to other TSP domains, the model shows an elongated three-stranded fold stabilized by disulfide bonds at both ends (Ayadi, 2008; Tan et al., 2002).
evidence: This claim is supported by the structural model shown in Figure 1A and citations to prior structural studies.

claim: Two positively charged grooves (Site-1 and Site-2) on one face of the RSPO3 TSP/BR domain model suggest potential sites of interaction with negatively charged HS polymers.
source: Two positively charged grooves (Site-1 and Site-2 in Figure 1A and Figure 1—video 1) on one face of the model suggested potential sites of interaction with negatively charged HS polymers.
evidence: This claim is supported by the structural model and electrostatic potential map shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Deleting the TSP/BR domain of RSPO3 reduced its potency by 82-fold in WT HAP1-7TGP cells.
source: As we had observed previously (see Figure 2F and G from Lebensohn and Rohatgi, 2018), deleting the TSP/BR domain of RSPO3 reduced its potency by 82-fold in WT HAP1-7TGP cells (Figure 1D)
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D and citation to prior work.

claim: Deleting the TSP/BR domain of RSPO3 completely abolished signaling in LGR4/5/6KO cells.
source: and completely abolished signaling in LGR4/5/6KO cells (Figure 1E).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: The K/R→E mutations in the TSP/BR domain of RSPO3 reduced its potency by 13-fold in WT HAP1-7TGP cells.
source: Similarly, the K/R→E mutations we introduced into the TSP/BR domain of RSPO3 reduced its potency by 13-fold in WT HAP1-7TGP cells (Figure 1D)
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: The K/R→E mutations in the TSP/BR domain of RSPO3 almost completely abolished its ability to potentiate WNT signaling in LGR4/5/6KO cells.
source: and almost completely abolished its ability to potentiate WNT signaling in LGR4/5/6KO cells (Figure 1E).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: Interactions between basic K and R residues in the TSP/BR domain of RSPO3 and the HS chains of HSPGs contribute substantially to potentiating WNT signaling in the presence of LGRs.
source: Our data supports the model that interactions between basic K and R residues in the TSP/BR domain of RSPO3 and the HS chains of HSPGs contribute substantially to potentiating WNT signaling in the presence of LGRs.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from mutagenesis experiments shown in Figure 1.

claim: In the absence of LGRs, the RSPO3-HSPG interaction becomes essential to potentiate WNT signaling.
source: In the absence of LGRs, the RSPO3-HSPG interaction becomes essential to potentiate WNT signaling.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing loss of signaling in LGR4/5/6KO cells when HSPG binding is disrupted.

claim: HS20 is an scFv antibody selected by phage display to bind to the HS chains of GPC3.
source: We engineered a synthetic RSPO3 protein in which we replaced the entire TSP/BR domain with HS20, an scFv antibody selected by phage display to bind to the HS chains of GPC3 (Gao et al., 2016; Gao et al., 2014; Geoghegan et al., 2017; Figure 2A and Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: Replacing the TSP/BR domain with HS20 in RSPO3 ΔTSP/BR HS20 did not disrupt the ability of RSPO3 to signal both in the presence and absence of LGRs.
source: Replacing the TSP/BR domain with HS20 in RSPO3 ΔTSP/BR HS20 did not disrupt the ability of RSPO3 to signal both in the presence and absence of LGRs (Figure 2C and D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C and D.

claim: Mutations in the antigen-binding CDR3 of HS20 entirely eliminated the WNT-potentiating activity of RSPO3 ΔTSP/BR HS20, both in the presence and absence of LGRs.
source: Importantly, mutations in the antigen-binding third complementarity-determining region (CDR3) of HS20 (RSPO3 ΔTSP/BR HS20 (GS) and RSPO3 ΔTSP/BR HS20 (A) in Figure 2A and B) entirely eliminated the WNT-potentiating activity of RSPO3 ΔTSP/BR HS20, both in the presence and absence of LGRs (Figure 2E and F).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2E and F.

claim: HS20 can functionally substitute for the TSP/BR domain of RSPO3.
source: The fact that HS20, a structurally unrelated protein specifically selected for HS-binding activity (Gao et al., 2014), can functionally substitute for the TSP/BR domain of RSPO3 provides strong support for our model that interactions with HSPGs are required to potentiate WNT signaling in cells lacking LGRs, and also contribute significantly in cells containing LGRs.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing functional equivalence of HS20 and TSP/BR domain.

claim: Point mutations (R67A/Q72A) in the FU1 domain of RSPO3 ΔTSP/BR HS20 reduced signaling potency by 10-fold in WT HAP1-7TGP cells.
source: Point mutations (R67A/Q72A) in the FU1 domain of RSPO3 ΔTSP/BR HS20 (RSPO3 ΔTSP/BR HS20 (R67A/Q72A) in Figure 2A and B) known to weaken the interaction with ZNRF3/RNF43 (Xie et al., 2013), reduced signaling potency by 10-fold in WT HAP1-7TGP cells (Figure 2G)
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2G and citation to prior work.

claim: Point mutations (R67A/Q72A) in the FU1 domain of RSPO3 ΔTSP/BR HS20 abolished signaling in LGR4/5/6KO cells.
source: and abolished signaling in LGR4/5/6KO cells (Figure 2H).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2H.

claim: Point mutations (F106E/F110E) in the FU2 domain of RSPO3 ΔTSP/BR HS20 reduced signaling efficacy by 80% and potency by 3-fold in WT HAP1-7TGP cells.
source: Point mutations (F106E/F110E) in the FU2 domain of RSPO3 ΔTSP/BR HS20 (RSPO3 ΔTSP/BR HS20 (F106E/F110E) in Figure 2A and B) that weaken interactions with LGRs (Xie et al., 2013) reduced signaling efficacy by 80% and potency by 3-fold in WT HAP1-7TGP cells (Figure 2G).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2G and citation to prior work.

claim: Disrupting the LGR-binding FU2 domain in RSPO3 ΔTSP/BR HS20 (F106E/F110E) did not reduce signaling in LGR4/5/6KO cells.
source: As expected, disrupting the LGR-binding FU2 domain in RSPO3 ΔTSP/BR HS20 (F106E/F110E) did not reduce signaling in LGR4/5/6KO cells (Figure 2H).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2H.

claim: Interactions with ZNRF3/RNF43, LGRs and HSPGs all contribute to the potentiation of WNT signaling by RSPO3 ΔTSP/BR HS20 in the presence of LGRs.
source: We conclude that interactions with ZNRF3/RNF43, LGRs and HSPGs all contribute to the potentiation of WNT signaling by RSPO3 ΔTSP/BR HS20 in the presence of LGRs.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from mutational analysis shown in Figure 2.

claim: Interactions with ZNRF3/RNF43 and HSPGs are required for signaling in the absence of LGRs.
source: Interactions with ZNRF3/RNF43 and HSPGs are required for signaling in the absence of LGRs.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from mutational analysis shown in Figure 2.

claim: RSPO3 can bind simultaneously to LGR and HSPG co-receptors, which together present the ligand to ZNRF3/RNF43.
source: The simplest model to explain these results is that RSPO3 can bind simultaneously to LGR and HSPG co-receptors, which together present the ligand to ZNRF3/RNF43, the key effectors that mediate endocytosis of the complex.
evidence: This claim is a model proposed based on inference from experimental data.

claim: Without LGRs, RSPO3 is presented by HSPGs alone, explaining the significantly lower potency of both WT RSPO3 and RSPO3 ΔTSP/BR HS20 in LGR4/5/6KO compared to WT HAP1-7TGP cells.
source: Without LGRs, RSPO3 is presented by HSPGs alone, explaining the significantly lower potency of both WT RSPO3 and RSPO3 ΔTSP/BR HS20 in LGR4/5/6KO compared to WT HAP1-7TGP cells (Figures 1D, E, 2C and D).
evidence: This claim is a model proposed based on inference from experimental data shown in Figures 1 and 2.

claim: Treatment of either WT HAP1-7TGP or LGR4/5/6KO cells with WT RSPO3 led to the depletion of RNF43-Flag from the cell surface and a reduction in its total cellular level.
source: Treatment of either WT HAP1-7TGP or LGR4/5/6KO cells with WT RSPO3 led to the depletion of RNF43-Flag from the cell surface and a reduction in its total cellular level (Figure 3A and B)
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A and B.

claim: LGR-dependent and LGR-independent potentiation of WNT signaling by RSPO3 proceed through similar mechanisms.
source: Treatment of either WT HAP1-7TGP or LGR4/5/6KO cells with WT RSPO3 led to the depletion of RNF43-Flag from the cell surface and a reduction in its total cellular level (Figure 3A and B), suggesting similar signaling mechanisms for LGR-dependent and LGR-independent potentiation of WNT signaling.
evidence: This claim is inferred from experimental data showing similar effects on RNF43 in both cell types.

claim: The ZNRF3/RNF43-interacting FU1 domain is essential for RSPO3 signaling in cells lacking LGRs.
source: These results are consistent with our previous mutational analysis demonstrating that the ZNRF3/RNF43-interacting FU1 domain is essential for RSPO3 signaling in cells lacking LGRs (Lebensohn and Rohatgi, 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Deletion of the TSP/BR domain of RSPO3 prevented the internalization and degradation of RNF43-Flag in both WT HAP1-7TGP and LGR4/5/6KO cells.
source: Deletion of the TSP/BR domain of RSPO3 (RSPO3 ΔTSP/BR in Figure 3A and B) prevented the internalization and degradation of RNF43-Flag in both WT HAP1-7TGP and LGR4/5/6KO cells
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A and B.

claim: Addition of RSPO3 ΔTSP/BR HS20 to either WT HAP1-7TGP or LGR4/5/6KO cells resulted in the depletion of RNF43-Flag from the cell surface and a reduction in its total cellular level.
source: In contrast, as with WT RSPO3, addition of RSPO3 ΔTSP/BR HS20 to either WT HAP1-7TGP (Figure 3A) or LGR4/5/6KO (Figure 3B) cells resulted in the depletion of RNF43-Flag from the cell surface and a reduction in its total cellular level.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A and B.

claim: The effects of RSPO3 ΔTSP/BR HS20 on RNF43 internalization and degradation were dependent on the interaction between HS20 and HS chains.
source: The effects of RSPO3 ΔTSP/BR HS20 were dependent on the interaction between HS20 and HS chains, since the RSPO3 ΔTSP/BR HS20 (GS) mutant, which carries mutations in the HS-binding CDR3 loop of HS20, failed to promote internalization and degradation of RNF43-Flag (Figure 3A and B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A and B.

claim: HSPGs represent the third major class of RSPO co-receptors, in addition to LGRs and ZNRF3/RNF43.
source: We propose that HSPGs represent the third major class of RSPO co-receptors, in addition to LGRs and ZNRF3/RNF43.
evidence: This claim is a conclusion based on the experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Cell-surface HSPGs comprise six glypicans (GPC1-6), which are anchored to the plasma membrane by a glycophosphatidylinositol (GPI) linkage, and four syndecans (SDC1-4), which are single pass transmembrane proteins.
source: Cell-surface HSPGs comprise six glypicans (GPC1-6), which are anchored to the plasma membrane by a glycophosphatidylinositol (GPI) linkage, and four syndecans (SDC1-4), which are single pass transmembrane proteins (Sarrazin et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by established knowledge and citation.

claim: RSPO3 can use the HS chains on multiple HSPGs to potentiate WNT signaling.
source: In our previous eLife paper (Lebensohn and Rohatgi, 2018), we presented evidence that RSPO3 can use the HS chains on multiple HSPGs to potentiate WNT signaling.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: HS20 bound equally well to GPC3 and GPC4.
source: In a binding assay with purified proteins, HS20 bound equally well to GPC3 and GPC4 (Figure 4A)
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: HS20 failed to bind to mutant GPC3 and GPC4 proteins that cannot be modified by HS chains.
source: HS20 failed to bind to mutant GPC3 and GPC4 proteins that cannot be modified by HS chains (GPC3ΔHS and GPC4ΔHS in Figure 4A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: HS20 recognizes the HS side-chain structure shared by multiple HSPGs, rather than binding to the protein core of a specific GPC.
source: These results support a prior conclusion that HS20 recognizes the HS side-chain structure shared by multiple HSPGs, rather than binding to the protein core of a specific GPC (Gao et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data and citation to prior work.

claim: Disrupting GPC3 in LGR4/5/6KO cells had no significant effect on signaling induced by either WT RSPO3 or RSPO3 ΔTSP/BR HS20.
source: Disrupting GPC3 in LGR4/5/6KO cells had no significant effect on signaling induced by either WT RSPO3 or RSPO3 ΔTSP/BR HS20 (Figure 4B and C)
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B and C.

claim: Disrupting GPC4 or PIGL modestly reduced the potency of both WT RSPO3 and RSPO3 ΔTSP/BR HS20.
source: Disrupting GPC4 or PIGL modestly reduced the potency (i.e. increased the EC50) of both WT RSPO3 and RSPO3 ΔTSP/BR HS20 (Figure 4B and C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B and C.

claim: Combined disruption of all SDCs increased the potency of both WT RSPO3 and RSPO3 ΔTSP/BR HS20.
source: Combined disruption of all SDCs – SDC1, SDC2, SDC3 and SDC4 – surprisingly increased the potency (ie. lowered the EC50) of both WT RSPO3 and RSPO3 ΔTSP/BR HS20 (Figure 4B and C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B and C.

claim: Some SDCs inhibit WNT/β-catenin signaling through regulation of LRP6 and RSPO3.
source: This increase in potency may be related to the previous observation that some SDCs inhibit WNT/β-catenin signaling through regulation of LRP6 and RSPO3 (Astudillo et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Disrupting EXTL3 impaired signaling by both WT RSPO3 and RSPO3 ΔTSP/BR HS20 to the greatest extent.
source: Finally, disrupting EXTL3, predicted to globally block HS chain biosynthesis, impaired signaling by both proteins to the greatest extent (Figure 4B and C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B and C.

claim: RSPO3 ΔTSP/BR HS20, like WT RSPO3, can signal in a redundant manner via either GPCs, SDCs or another HSPG by engaging their HS chains rather than their protein cores.
source: These results are most consistent with the model that RSPO3 ΔTSP/BR HS20, like WT RSPO3, can signal in a redundant manner via either GPCs, SDCs or another HSPG by engaging their HS chains rather than their protein cores.
evidence: This claim is a model inferred from experimental data on HSPG specificity.

claim: The growth of mouse small intestinal organoids is strictly dependent on exogenously supplied RSPOs.
source: The growth of mouse small intestinal organoids is strictly dependent on exogenously supplied RSPOs (Sato et al., 2009)
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: The growth of mouse small intestinal organoids is dependent on the expression of LGRs.
source: and on the expression of LGRs (de Lau et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Depletion of HS chains in the intestinal epithelium compromises WNT-dependent crypt renewal and regeneration following radiation-induced injury.
source: In addition, studies in mice have shown that depletion of HS chains in the intestinal epithelium compromise WNT-dependent crypt renewal and regeneration following radiation-induced injury (Yamamoto et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: WT RSPO3 promoted the growth of intestinal organoids with multiple budded structures at concentrations down to 0.5 nM.
source: WT RSPO3 promoted the growth of intestinal organoids with multiple budded structures at concentrations down to 0.5 nM (Figure 5A and B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5A and B.

claim: The buds in intestinal organoids represent crypt domains, enriched in markers of proliferating cells (Ki67) and of Paneth cells (lysozyme).
source: The buds represent crypt domains, since they are enriched in markers of proliferating cells (Ki67) and of Paneth cells (lysozyme) (Figure 5C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: RSPO3 ΔTSP/BR was markedly less potent than WT RSPO3 in promoting organoid growth, enabling only a few organoids to grow at a concentration of 10 nM.
source: RSPO3 ΔTSP/BR was markedly less potent in this assay, enabling only a few organoids to grow at a concentration of 10 nM (Figure 5B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: RSPO3 ΔTSP/BR HS20 was more potent than WT RSPO3 in supporting organoid growth, supporting some organoid growth even at concentrations as low as 0.1 nM.
source: Not only was RSPO3 ΔTSP/BR HS20 able to fully support organoid growth, with budding of normal crypt domains, but it was more potent than WT RSPO3, supporting some organoid growth even at concentrations as low as 0.1 nM (Figure 5A and B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5A and B.

claim: Organoids grown in the presence of RSPO3 ΔTSP/BR HS20 were indistinguishable from those grown in the presence of WT RSPO3, with crypt domains containing proliferating cells and Paneth cells.
source: Organoids grown in the presence of RSPO3 ΔTSP/BR HS20 were indistinguishable from those grown in the presence of WT RSPO3, with crypt domains containing proliferating cells and Paneth cells (Figure 5C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: The capacity of RSPO3 ΔTSP/BR HS20 to promote organoid growth required the interaction between HS20 and HS chains.
source: The capacity of RSPO3 ΔTSP/BR HS20 to promote organoid growth required the interaction between HS20 and HS chains, since RSPO3 ΔTSP/BR HS20 (GS), carrying mutations in the HS-binding CDR3 loop (Figure 2A) failed to promote organoid growth at concentrations below 10 nM, similarly to RSPO3 ΔTSP/BR (Figure 5A and B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5A and B.

claim: The interaction between the TSP/BR domain, or HS20, and HSPGs contributes substantially to the capacity of RSPO3 to support the growth of mouse intestinal organoids.
source: We conclude from these experiments that the interaction between the TSP/BR domain, or HS20, and HSPGs contributes substantially to the capacity of RSPO3 to support the growth of mouse intestinal organoids.
evidence: This claim is a conclusion based on experimental data from organoid experiments.

claim: Gpc3 mRNA expression in mouse intestinal organoids is undetectable.
source: While additional work will be required to establish which specific HSPGs mediate RSPO reception in the intestine, we note that Gpc3 mRNA expression in mouse intestinal organoids is undetectable (Lindeboom et al., 2018)
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: GPC4, SDC1 and SDC4 are expressed at detectable levels in mouse intestinal organoids.
source: Multi-omics data shows that GPC4, SDC1 and SDC4 are expressed at detectable levels in mouse intestinal organoids (Lindeboom et al., 2018), making them candidate receptors for RSPO3 in this tissue.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: The RSPO3 screen in LGR4/5/6KO cells revealed a subset of the WNT signaling regulators previously identified in the RSPO1 screen in WT HAP1-7TGP cells.
source: The RSPO3 screen in LGR4/5/6KO cells revealed a subset of the WNT signaling regulators previously identified in the RSPO1 screen in WT HAP1-7TGP cells (Figure 6A–C and Supplementary files 4 and 5)
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from genetic screens shown in Figure 6.

claim: LGR4 was not a significant hit in the RSPO3 screen in LGR4/5/6KO cells.
source: LGR4, the top hit of the RSPO1 screen in WT HAP1-7TGP cells, was not a significant hit in the RSPO3 screen in LGR4/5/6KO cells, in which LGR4 had been disrupted by CRISPR/Cas9-mediated genome editing (Figure 6A–C and Supplementary files 4 and 5).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from genetic screens shown in Figure 6.

claim: The RSPO3 screen in LGR4/5/6KO cells failed to reveal any unique significant hits compared to the RSPO1 screen in WT HAP1-7TGP cells.
source: The RSPO3 screen in LGR4/5/6KO cells failed to reveal any unique significant hits compared to the RSPO1 screen in WT HAP1-7TGP cells (Figure 6A–C and Supplementary files 4 and 5)
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from genetic screens shown in Figure 6.

claim: There were no genes selectively required for LGR-independent potentiation of WNT signaling by RSPO3.
source: suggesting there were no genes selectively required for LGR-independent potentiation of WNT signaling by RSPO3.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the lack of unique hits in the RSPO3 screen.

claim: Components of the GPI-anchor biosynthetic machinery and GPC4 were hits in both screens due to the requirement of GPI-anchored GPCs for low-level WNT signaling, independently of RSPOs.
source: While several components of the GPI-anchor biosynthetic machinery, including PIGP, PIGS, PIGU, PIGL and DPM3, as well as GPC4 were hits in both screens, we have previously shown that their presence as significant hits in the RSPO1 screen in WT HAP1-7TGP cells was due to the requirement of GPI-anchored GPCs for low-level WNT signaling, independently of RSPOs (Lebensohn et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Haploid genetic screens did not reveal an additional co-receptor required for LGR-independent potentiation of WNT signaling by RSPO3.
source: In summary, haploid genetic screens did not reveal an additional co-receptor required for LGR-independent potentiation of WNT signaling by RSPO3.
evidence: This claim is a conclusion based on experimental data from genetic screens.

claim: The TSP/BR domain of RSPOs is conserved across vertebrates, primitive chordates and hemichordates.
source: The TSP/BR domain of RSPOs is conserved across vertebrates, primitive chordates and hemichordates, suggesting a functional role in signaling by these ligands (de Lau et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: A fragment of RSPOs that contains only the FU1 and FU2 domains can amplify WNT/β-catenin signaling in vitro.
source: Initial studies showed that this domain was dispensable, since a fragment of RSPOs that contains only the FU1 and FU2 domains can amplify WNT/β-catenin signaling in vitro (Glinka et al., 2011; Kazanskaya et al., 2004; Kim et al., 2008; Zebisch et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: The TSP/BR domain of RSPO3 is essential for signaling in the absence of LGRs.
source: Our previous (Lebensohn and Rohatgi, 2018) and current work provides a clear function for the TSP/BR domain of RSPO3 in WNT/β-catenin signaling in vitro and ex vivo: (1) it is essential for signaling in the absence of LGRs
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from current and prior work.

claim: The TSP/BR domain of RSPO3 enhances signaling potency in the presence of LGRs in both cultured cells and intestinal organoids.
source: and (2) it enhances signaling potency in the presence of LGRs in both cultured cells and intestinal organoids.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from current work.

claim: Only RSPO2 and RSPO3, but not RSPO1 or RSPO4, bind to SDC1-4.
source: It will be interesting to determine whether the TSP/BR domains of RSPO1 and RSPO4 can also enhance ligand potency, especially in light of the observation that only RSPO2 and RSPO3, but not RSPO1 or RSPO4, bind to SDC1-4 (Ohkawara et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: HSPGs and HS chains were initially implicated in the distribution, stability and potency of WNT ligands in studies from Drosophila.
source: HSPGs and HS chains were initially implicated in the distribution, stability and potency of WNT ligands in studies from Drosophila, which lacks an RSPO signaling module for WNT amplification (Baeg et al., 2001; Reichsman et al., 1996).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: HSPGs promoted WNT/β-catenin signaling by directly binding to WNT ligands in Drosophila studies.
source: In those studies, HSPGs promoted WNT/β-catenin signaling by directly binding to WNT ligands.
evidence: This claim is supported by established knowledge from prior studies.

claim: Depletion of HS chains by genetic disruption of enzymes required for their synthesis impairs WNT/β-catenin signaling in the mouse intestine, the mouse mammary gland and in multiple myeloma cells.
source: However, depletion of HS chains by the genetic disruption of enzymes required for their synthesis has also been shown to impair WNT/β-catenin signaling and associated responses in the mouse intestine, the mouse mammary gland and in multiple myeloma cells, all contexts in which RSPOs play prominent roles (Alexander et al., 2000; Ren et al., 2018; Yamamoto et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: Impaired WNT reception is the reason why genes encoding proteins required for the biogenesis of GPCs, and GPC4, were prominent hits in both RSPO screens.
source: In fact, we showed previously (Lebensohn et al., 2016; Lebensohn and Rohatgi, 2018) that impaired WNT reception is the reason why genes encoding proteins required for the biogenesis of GPCs, and GPC4, the most abundant GPC in HAP1 cells, were prominent hits in both of our RSPO screens (Figure 6A–C and Supplementary files 4 and 5).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work and data from Figure 6.

claim: RSPO mutagenesis and engineering experiments cleanly demonstrate that interactions with HSPGs are required for RSPO reception.
source: Our present RSPO mutagenesis and engineering experiments, which leave the HSPG repertoire of cells intact and their role in WNT reception undisturbed, cleanly demonstrate that interactions with HSPGs are also required for RSPO reception.
evidence: This claim is a conclusion based on experimental data from the current study.

claim: Exogenously added heparin inhibits, rather than promotes, RSPO signaling.
source: First, exogenously added heparin inhibits, rather than promotes, RSPO signaling (Lebensohn and Rohatgi, 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: The mere interaction between RSPOs and HSPGs seems to be sufficient for signaling.
source: Instead, the mere interaction between RSPOs and HSPGs seems to be sufficient for signaling.
evidence: This claim is inferred from experimental data showing functional substitution of TSP/BR with HS20.

claim: Both WT RSPO3 and RSPO3 ΔTSP/BR HS20 can cause internalization and degradation of RNF43-Flag in cells lacking LGRs.
source: Our results directly demonstrate that both WT RSPO3 and RSPO3 ΔTSP/BR HS20 can cause internalization and degradation of RNF43-Flag in cells lacking LGRs (Figure 3B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Clearance of ZNRF3 and RNF43 from the cell surface induced by RSPO3-HSPG interactions would be sufficient to enhance WNT signaling.
source: Since ZNRF3 and RNF43 are E3 ubiquitin ligases that negatively regulate WNT receptors, their clearance from the cell surface induced by RSPO3-HSPG interactions would be sufficient to enhance WNT signaling.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the known function of ZNRF3/RNF43 and experimental data.

claim: The affinity of the FU2 domain for LGRs is high (in the nM range) for all RSPOs.
source: The affinity of the FU2 domain for LGRs is high (in the nM range) for all RSPOs, while the affinity of the FU1 domain for ZNRF3/RNF43 is much higher for RSPO2 and RSPO3 compared to RSPO1 and RSPO4 (Zebisch et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: The interaction with LGRs is not sufficient to drive the efficient endocytosis of RNF43 for RSPO3.
source: At least for RSPO3, our experiments suggest that the interaction with LGRs is not sufficient to drive the efficient endocytosis of RNF43.
evidence: This claim is inferred from experimental data showing requirement for HSPG binding.

claim: HSPG binding is required for RSPO3 signaling even in the presence of LGRs.
source: HSPG binding, provided by the native TSP/BR domain or by the non-native HS20 scFv, is also required even in the presence of LGRs (Figure 3A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: LGRs are insufficient to mediate RSPO signaling for RSPO3 and RSPO2.
source: In the case of RSPO3 and also RSPO2, not only are LGRs insufficient to mediate RSPO signaling, but they are in fact dispensable.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from current and prior work.

claim: The higher affinity of RSPO2 and RSPO3 for ZNRF3/RNF43 is the reason LGRs are dispensable for these RSPOs.
source: This is most likely due to the higher affinity of these RSPO ligands for ZNRF3/RNF43, since replacing the ZNRF3/RNF43-bindnig FU1 domain of RSPO1 with that of RSPO3 is sufficient to render RSPO1 capable of signaling without LGRs (Lebensohn and Rohatgi, 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work and inference.

claim: HSPGs can markedly enhance the potency of RSPO3 even when LGRs are present.
source: However, even when LGRs are present, HSPGs can markedly enhance the potency of RSPO3 (Figure 1D and Figure 5A and B) and potentially other RSPOs.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 1D and 5A-B.

claim: HSPGs may trap RSPOs near the cell surface, increasing their local concentration and the extent of their binding to LGRs.
source: One possibility is that HSPGs trap RSPOs near the cell surface, increasing their local concentration and the extent of their binding to LGRs.
evidence: This claim is a speculative model proposed by the authors.

claim: Either the genetic or enzymatic depletion of HS chains, or the removal of the TSP/BR domain, reduces binding of RSPOs to the surface of multiple myeloma cells, while the genetic depletion of LGR4 does not.
source: This model is supported by the observation that either the genetic or enzymatic depletion of HS chains, or the removal of the TSP/BR domain, reduces binding of RSPOs to the surface of multiple myeloma cells, while the genetic depletion of LGR4 does not (Ren et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: The simultaneous binding of RSPO3 to LGRs and HSPGs may be required to trigger efficient endocytosis.
source: Alternatively, the simultaneous binding of RSPO3 to LGRs and HSPGs may be required to trigger efficient endocytosis.
evidence: This claim is a speculative model proposed by the authors.

claim: HSPGs are multiply redundant in HAP1 cells.
source: We did not identify a single HSPG that serves as the RSPO receptor in HAP1 cells, most likely because HSPGs are multiply redundant in these cells (Lebensohn and Rohatgi, 2018).
evidence: This claim is inferred from experimental data and citation to prior work.

claim: The interaction of SDC4 and RSPO3 regulates WNT/planar cell polarity (PCP) signaling during Xenopus gastrulation by a process that requires clathrin-mediated endocytosis.
source: For instance, the interaction of SDC4 and RSPO3 was shown to regulate WNT/planar cell polarity (PCP) signaling during Xenopus gastrulation by a process that requires clathrin-mediated endocytosis (Ohkawara et al., 2011)
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: SDC1 promotes signaling in multiple myeloma by presenting WNTs and RSPOs.
source: and SDC1 was shown to promote signaling in multiple myeloma by presenting WNTs and RSPOs (Ren et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work.
